project_name: Pinecrest Mill kraft lignin cake (fictional): dashboard assessment
disclaimers: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.
BioValue AI gives indicative decision support. It does not guarantee profitability, does not verify customer demand, and does not constitute engineering approval.

Gross margin, profitability, NPV, and IRR are not calculated. They need capital costs, fixed costs, a discount rate, a time horizon, and agreed definitions, none of which are available yet. Gross contribution excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the value of the feedstock in its current use.
Scores use a 1-5 scale. A criterion that was not assessed lowers data completeness; it is never counted as a low score.

constraints: The lignin is currently used as internal boiler fuel, so commercial diversion would affect that existing use.
The stream leaves as wet cake and no lignin dryer is available; buyers requiring dry powder would need drying capability.
Solvent or membrane fractionation and chemical modification are not available at the mill.
Moisture is uncertain and affects dry tonnage and shipped mass.
Missing molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl, and sodium data limit comparison with pathway or buyer specifications.
data_quality_notes: The record is fictional demo data; all figures are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from a real mill.
The lignin assay method is stated only for illustration, so the reported lignin content needs confirmation against a defined method.
Moisture is uncertain; the record recommends measuring it over time.
The recorded annual quantity, moisture, dry matter, and composition include assumed ranges reflecting variability.
agent.summary: The validated demo profile records 5,000.0 t/yr wet lignin cake at a moisture fraction of 0.6, corresponding to 2,000.0 t/yr dry mass. The dry-matter balance and composition-total checks passed; three composition properties are missing. Do not use these fictional assumptions for real commercial decisions.

lignin_pct.method: Acid-insoluble (Klason) plus acid-soluble lignin, as % of dry matter (method stated for illustration)

sulfur_pct.method: Total sulfur by elemental analysis (stated for illustration)

carbohydrates_pct.method: Total sugars after acid hydrolysis (stated for illustration)

checks.detail: recorded dry matter 2,000 t/yr; wet quantity x (1 - moisture) = 2,000 t/yr
lignin + ash + carbohydrates = 96.5% of dry matter
3 missing figure(s), each with a data-gap entry

data_gaps.impact: Every figure in this profile is invented for demonstration. Results based on it say nothing about a real mill.
data_gaps.next_step: Replace the profile with the mill's own lab data and production records.

data_gaps.impact: Molecular weight can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of molecular weight distribution, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: Phenolic hydroxyl content can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of hydroxyl group content, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: The make-up of the ash is unknown, so ash-related requirements can only be checked against total ash.
data_gaps.next_step: Request an inorganic element analysis of the ash.

data_gaps.impact: Reported lignin content depends on what the analysis counts. The method here is stated for illustration only.
data_gaps.next_step: Confirm the analytical method with the lab and use the same one when comparing with buyers' specifications.

data_gaps.impact: Moisture sets the dry tonnage (dry matter = wet quantity x (1 - moisture)) and the mass that has to be shipped.
data_gaps.next_step: Log cake moisture for each shift over at least one month.

checks.disclaimer: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.

current_use.description: Fictional: the precipitated lignin is fired in the mill's own boilers in place of purchased fuel. The unit was built to relieve the recovery boiler, not to sell lignin.

geographic_market.logistics: Fictional: rail siding at the mill; the nearest deep-water port is assumed to be about 150 km away.

supported_claims.EV-PF-01#1: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#2: Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#R1: Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#2: UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
supported_claims.EV-PF-04#2: With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#4: Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#1: UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#3: UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#3: A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin can partially replace phenol in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins for wood-panel adhesives, but activation or depolymerization may be needed.
Lignin-phenol-formaldehyde resin is documented for veneer plywood, with a laboratory study also testing poplar plywood.

target_customers.statement: Plywood and other wood-based-panel producers are the implied customers for lignin-based PF adhesives.

competing_materials.statement: Phenol in PF resin is the incumbent material being partially replaced.

qualification_requirements.statement: UPM reports its LPF resin meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood and provides formaldehyde-emissions measurements under EN 717-2.

A laboratory study reports that resin with depolymerized lignin at 50% of the phenolic component met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in that study; the paper names the standard inconsistently.
Kraft lignin requires activation or depolymerization before PF-resin use; the review describes a typical replacement level of up to 50% for a two-step process using depolymerized lignin.

limitations: UPM's performance and cost statements are vendor claims without cited test reports; the source does not state that its lignin is kraft lignin or provide its composition (EV-PF-02).
The review's replacement levels summarize studies rather than a single commercial plant, and its TRL 8 rating applies to biobased phenolic resins generally, not specifically kraft lignin (EV-PF-01).
The oxidative-depolymerization results are from a laboratory study with poplar plywood, and the cited standard is named inconsistently (EV-PF-04).
Pinecrest's molecular weight and phenolic hydroxyl data are missing, and the mill has no chemical-modification capability, limiting confirmation of fit to the reported pretreatment and resin process.
EV-PF-03's economic estimate is per marginal tonne of pulp, not per tonne of lignin, and additional operating costs are unknown.
missing_information: No named buyers, lignin purchase prices, sales volumes, contract terms, or regional demand estimates are provided.
Evidence does not establish that Pinecrest's untreated wet cake meets a buyer's resin specifications or quantify the drying, activation, or depolymerization investment needed.
The evidence does not establish commercial sales specifically of Pinecrest-like kraft lignin; vendor-reported industrial proof is not an explicit sales record.

market_evidence.rationale: Evidence includes plywood performance results, a vendor claim of industrial proof, and broader development/readiness evidence, but does not document commercial sales by a lignin producer. This fits documented trials or development evidence rather than the rubric's sales-based level.

supported_claims.EV-PU-01#1: Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#2: Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.
supported_claims.EV-PU-02#1: Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#1: Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#3: Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#2: In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#R1: Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#R1: Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#2: Unmodified lignin reduced foam resiliency: compression set rose to 7-32% against 6% for the control, though it stayed within the standard's limit of below 60%.
supported_claims.EV-PU-05#1: Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin has been tested as a partial replacement for petroleum-based polyols in rigid PUR/PIR insulation foam, with outcomes varying by lignin and formulation.
Unmodified kraft lignin has also been tested in flexible polyurethane foam; the authors suggest denser, stiffer kraft-lignin foams may suit heavy-duty foam uses.
Reviewed studies report higher replacement levels for treated kraft lignin than for untreated lignin, including oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction routes.

target_customers.statement: Rigid insulation-foam producers are implied by the PUR/PIR foam tests and their ASTM type 1 specification context.
Flexible-foam producers serving automotive applications, and potentially heavy-duty foam producers, are implied by the flexible-foam study's applications discussion.

competing_materials.statement: Petroleum-based polyols are the incumbent material being partially replaced.

qualification_requirements.statement: The rigid-foam study assessed whether foams passed ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications; it reports that 16 of 19 tested lignins passed all measured specifications at 30 wt% polyol replacement, while two of the three failures used kraft lignin.
One study cites total hydroxyl value above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) as acceptable for rigid polyurethane foam; this is total OH, not phenolic OH.
The flexible-foam study reports compression set within the standard's limit of below 60% for its lignin foams, while also noting reduced resiliency versus the control.
The review states that kraft lignin needs significant treatment, such as oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction, to reach target polyurethane properties.

limitations: The rigid-foam trials were laboratory cup tests across several lignin types; the source does not provide a kraft-only pass rate, and the best performer was not kraft lignin (EV-PU-01).
The 2013 rigid-foam study was laboratory-scale, focused on high-density foam, and found kraft lignin insoluble in alcohols and only suspended in polyol, raising viscosity (EV-PU-02).
Flexible-foam results are laboratory one-pot foams; odor was not measured, despite being identified as a known drawback for some softwood kraft lignins (EV-PU-03).
The TRL and market figures in the review apply broadly to lignin polyurethane uses, not specifically to kraft-lignin foam; its market figures are dated (EV-PU-04).
The review on commercialization challenges was available only as an abstract (EV-PU-05).

Pinecrest lacks phenolic-OH and molecular-weight data and has no fractionation or chemical-modification capability; moisture and the need for drying are also unresolved for applications requiring dry feedstock.
missing_information: No named buyers, current lignin prices, purchase volumes, contract terms, or regional demand estimates are provided.
No evidence shows commercial sales of lignin-based polyurethane foam or a buyer qualification for Pinecrest's kraft lignin.
The evidence does not quantify the cost or mill infrastructure needed for drying, fractionation, or chemical modification of Pinecrest's wet cake.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents research studies and a review of development barriers, but no documented buyer, commercial sale, or buyer-facing pilot is reported for lignin-based polyurethane products. This matches the rubric's research-literature-only level.

supported_claims.EV-CM-01#1: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#3: None of the lignin samples in the study met the ORNL volatiles specification.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R1: Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R2: Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#1: A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#2: Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#1: Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#3: Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#2: Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#1: The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#2: The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#1: Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R1: Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R2: Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R3: Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R4: Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R5: Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#R1: Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin is discussed as a precursor for carbon fiber, but the cited work identifies demanding purity and processing needs and reports that tested samples failed the volatile-content specification.
Lignin-derived hard carbon is reviewed for sodium-ion battery anodes; the review reports a kraft-lignin comparison after carbonization at 1,200 °C.
Lignin can be converted to activated carbon, and one study reports that higher precursor ash reduced yield and carbon conversion.
A company announced a pilot line for lignin-based anode material for lithium-ion batteries, with scale-up plans described in the announcement.

target_customers.statement: Carbon-fiber producers and automotive lightweighting applications are implied by the carbon-fiber development project and its stated application focus.
Battery-material manufacturers, battery manufacturers, and carmakers are named or clearly implied for lignin-based anode material and qualification.

competing_materials.statement: PAN-based fiber is named as a competing carbon-fiber precursor; a project summary compares its estimated fiber cost with lignin-based fiber.
Anthracite is compared with lignin as a hard-carbon feedstock for sodium-ion batteries.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited ORNL carbon-fiber precursor specifications include lignin content greater than 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
The kraft lignin examined in a carbon-fiber report needed purification before use; the cited softwood-lignin discussion also says a plasticizing agent is needed for melt-spinning.
A company source says qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years; it gives no specific material test or quality specification.
The activated-carbon study reports no strict precursor-quality limits, while noting that lower ash improves yield.

limitations: Carbon-fiber precursor specifications are cited secondhand and do not apply to hard carbon or activated carbon; the study's lignin was not standard kraft lignin (EV-CM-01).

Carbon-fiber development findings are dated, and the GreenLight cost figures are modeled rather than measured; its TRL 5 applies to precursor-fiber production, not the full carbon-fiber chain (EV-CM-02; EV-CM-03).
The hard-carbon source is a review summarizing other studies and covers sodium-ion batteries; the feedstock cost basis is unspecified (EV-CM-04).
The activated-carbon results are from a laboratory study using zinc chloride activation (EV-CM-05).
The anode pilot announcement is company investor material with forward-looking statements; its later status was not verified, and it gives no lignin quality specifications (EV-CM-06).
Pinecrest's ash/sodium and other composition data are incomplete, and wet cake, uncertain moisture, lack of drying equipment, and the existing boiler-fuel use may affect pathway fit and diversion.
missing_information: No current buyer identities, purchase prices, contracted volumes, or regional demand estimates are documented.
There are no Pinecrest-specific qualification results for carbon fiber, battery anodes, or activated carbon, and no complete process-cost or capital estimate for converting its wet cake.

The carbon-materials evidence covers different products with distinct requirements; it does not establish a common specification or a single market opportunity across carbon fiber, hard carbon, and activated carbon.
The pilot announcement does not verify current operating status or establish sales to battery customers.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents industrially relevant precursor-fiber development and a company-announced anode pilot line, but it does not document commercial sales by a lignin producer to established buyers. This supports the rubric's trials, pilots, or development-partnership level.

processing_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin needs activation or depolymerization before use in phenol-formaldehyde resin.

The mill has no solvent or membrane fractionation or chemical-modification capability, and the stream leaves as wet cake without an available dryer; these are gaps to address if the chosen process or buyer requires them.
The deterministic feedstock-compatibility check could not produce a score because the evidence provides no numeric requirements for this pathway.

technical_maturity.statement: The evidence reports a TRL of 8 for producing biobased phenolic resins; the readiness tool maps this TRL to a score of 5.

adoption_barriers.statement: Pinecrest-specific untreated wet-cake qualification is unestablished, and buyer specifications, drying needs, and activation or depolymerization investment are not documented.

There are no named buyers or documented purchase prices, sales volumes, contract terms, or regional demand estimates; the available evidence describes resin applications and qualification results rather than Pinecrest sales.
Diversion would affect the lignin's existing use as internal boiler fuel.

missing_inputs: Buyer identities, purchase specifications, purchase volumes, and contract terms
Capital and operating costs for drying, activation, or depolymerization
assumptions: Economics tool scenarios assume wet feedstock mass of 4500.0 / 5000.0 / 5500.0 t/yr, moisture of 65.0 / 60.0 / 55.0% of wet mass, and availability of 40.0 / 50.0 / 60.0%; the tool identifies these as fictional assumptions.

Economics tool reports dry mass of 2000.0 t/yr (conservative 1575.0; optimistic 2475.0) and usable feedstock of 1000.0 t/yr (conservative 630.0; optimistic 1485.0), but cannot calculate product output, revenue, variable cost, or gross contribution without the missing inputs.
uncertainties: The evidence does not establish whether Pinecrest's lignin can meet a resin buyer's requirements or which pretreatment and drying configuration would be needed.
No product yield, price, or variable-cost inputs are available, so indicative gross contribution and economics score are unavailable.
No TRL claim specifically confirms readiness of a Pinecrest-specific process or formulation; the cited TRL is for biobased phenolic-resin production generally.

commercialization_feasibility.rationale: Major process capability gaps and buyer/qualification partners remain unidentified, matching the rubric level for a pathway needing major new assets and partners. The cited technology maturity supports a process route but does not resolve these mill-specific commercialization gaps.

feedstock_compatibility.rationale: The evidence library has no numeric requirements for this pathway to check against.

technical_readiness.rationale: TRL 8 maps to 5. Stated in EV-PF-01#3.

indicative_economics.rationale: Gross contribution per tonne could not be calculated. Missing inputs: product yield, product price, variable costs.

processing_requirements.statement: For carbon-fiber precursor, cited specifications include lignin content greater than 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm, volatile material below 5% at 250 °C, and removal of particulates larger than 1 µm; the examined kraft lignin also required purification.

The carbon-fiber compatibility tool returned score 1, based on its checked lignin-content and ash requirements; it states the result is for carbon fiber and other carbon products may have different requirements.

For activated carbon, the cited study gives no strict precursor-quality limits but says lower ash improves yield; hard-carbon and battery-anode applications have distinct requirements that are not established here.
The mill has no available dryer or chemical-modification capability; required purification and product-specific conversion would therefore need added capability or a partner.

technical_maturity.statement: The GreenLight project reports lignin precursor-fiber production advanced from TRL 2–3 to TRL 5; the readiness tool maps the cited TRL 5 to a score of 3.

adoption_barriers.statement: The cited carbon-fiber work identifies demanding purity and processing needs, and reports tested samples failed the volatile-content specification.
Battery-material and carmaker qualification can take 3 years according to a company source, which does not supply a specific test or material specification.

No Pinecrest-specific qualification, current buyer identities, purchase prices, contracted volumes, or complete conversion-cost estimate is available; the pilot announcement does not verify current operating status or sales.
The carbon-materials category spans products with distinct specifications and markets, so it does not establish one common specification or opportunity for Pinecrest.
Diversion would affect internal boiler-fuel use, and moisture is uncertain with no mill dryer available.

report.summary: Carbon materials is the sole ranked pathway under the scoring engine, but its rank is provisional: the compatibility score is low and economics are unassessed. Phenolic resins has strong general technical-readiness evidence, while polyurethane currently has weaker market evidence; neither can be ranked until missing feedstock-compatibility and economics inputs are addressed.

documented_facts.statement: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.
UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.
Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.
Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.
Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.

Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
Unmodified lignin reduced foam resiliency: compression set rose to 7-32% against 6% for the control, though it stayed within the standard's limit of below 60%.
Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
None of the lignin samples in the study met the ORNL volatiles specification.
Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).

The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
